Read this before you book anything

Two things that shape the whole weekend

1 — Monday 7 September is Labour Day

  • Busiest travel weekend of the Québec summer — both old towns will be shoulder-to-shoulder.
  • Accommodation sells out weeks ahead. Book now, not next week.
  • Westbound 401 into Toronto on Monday afternoon is the worst traffic of the year.

2 — Montréal first means Monday is the long haul

  • Québec City → home is 805 km, about 8h15 of pure driving.
  • With stops and holiday traffic, budget a 10–11 hour day.
  • The fix, and it is non-negotiable: leave by 07:00. Leave at 10:00 and you get home after 21:00.

The trade you are making

  • Easy Saturday (5h30) and gentle Sunday (2h45) — you pay for both on Monday.
  • Want to flip it? Québec City Saturday, Montréal Sunday, short drive home. The stop list simply runs in reverse.
The whole trip, in travel order

Every stop, one by one

All 47 stops in the exact order you will reach them, from pulling out of the driveway on Saturday to pulling back in on Monday. Numbers run straight through the weekend — nothing here is out of sequence. Sunday evening in Québec City doubles as the Goblin filming trail; those stops carry a plum tag.

Driving stop On foot Optional — cut if late Goblin filming location Must-visit — do not skip

If you only do fourteen things

Everything on this page is worth doing, but these fourteen are the ones that would make the weekend feel wasted if you missed them. They carry an amber ★ Must marker wherever they appear — on the timeline, on the city pages, on the food cards and on the photo spots.

Saturday: Thousand Islands Parkway · Notre-Dame Basilica · Place Jacques-Cartier · Kondiaronk Belvedere at sunset · smoked meat for dinner.
Sunday: St-Viateur bagels · Marché Jean-Talon · Montmorency Falls · Place Royale · Rue du Petit-Champlain · the Red Door · Château Frontenac · Terrasse Dufferin · Fontaine de Tourny at dusk.

The one genuine near-miss on that list is the Lévis ferry — twelve minutes and $4.50 for the best view in Québec. If Sunday evening runs ahead of schedule, add it.

Day 1 · Saturday 5 September Scarborough → Montréal 540 KM · 5H 30M
  1. 105:30ScarboroughDepart · Hwy 401 East · full tank
    Details

    HWY 401 EAST · FULL TANK BEFORE YOU GO

    Coffee in the car, bags in the night before. At 05:30 you are through Pickering and Oshawa in clear air. Leave at 08:00 on a long weekend instead and you will sit in it for an hour before you have left the GTA.

  2. ↓ 145 km · 1h 35m on the 401
  3. 207:15The Big Apple, ColborneExit 497 · breakfast & apple pie
    Details

    401 EXIT 497 · UNMISSABLE, IT IS A GIANT APPLE

    The most famous roadside stop in Ontario and a genuinely good bakery — apple pie, apple fritters, apple dumplings, all made on site. Check the opening time before you count on it; the bakery typically opens around 08:00. If you are too early, roll 20 minutes further to Brighton or Trenton for a diner breakfast instead.

  4. ↓ 115 km · 1h 10m
  5. 309:15KingstonSpringer Market Square · waterfront · Fort Henry
    Details

    SPRINGER MARKET SQUARE · CITY HALL · WATERFRONT

    The limestone city, and the best place on the whole drive to stretch properly. Park near Springer Market Square behind City Hall — Saturday is market day, so there will be produce, bread and buskers. Walk five minutes to the waterfront for the Lake Ontario view, then look up at Fort Henry on the hill across the causeway. Give it 45–60 minutes.

  6. ↓ 30 km · 30m
  7. 410:30Thousand Islands ParkwayScenic detour · Gananoque → Mallorytown
    Details

    EXIT THE 401 AT GANANOQUE, REJOIN AT MALLORYTOWN

    Do not stay on the 401 here. The parkway runs parallel for about 35 km directly along the St. Lawrence, past hundreds of tiny granite islands with cottages on them. It costs you almost no extra time and it is the prettiest half hour of the weekend. Pull off at any of the free riverside lookouts. If you want the postcard view from above, the 1000 Islands Skydeck on Hill Island is a short bridge hop — but the free roadside stops are honestly enough.

  8. ↓ 105 km · 1h 05m
  9. 512:00Upper Canada Village, MorrisburgOptional · save it for Monday's drive home
    Details

    MORRISBURG · CUT THIS IF YOU WANT MONTRÉAL BY 14:00

    A working 1860s village with costumed interpreters, plus another gorgeous riverside parkway that island-hops across the St. Lawrence. It is genuinely good — but it is a two-hour commitment on a day when Montréal is the prize. Save it for the drive home on Monday instead, where it makes a perfect lunch break.

  10. ↓ 80 km · 50m
  11. 612:45CornwallLast Ontario fuel · border 25 min away
    Details

    FILL UP HERE · QUÉBEC BORDER IS 25 MINUTES AWAY

    Gas is usually a few cents cheaper on the Ontario side, and with 4 adults and a full trunk you will want a topped tank going into the city. Quick washroom-and-snack stop, nothing more. No time-zone change at the border — Québec is on Eastern Time exactly like Ontario.

  12. ↓ 115 km · 1h 15m · into Québec
  13. 714:00Montréal — park the carChamp-de-Mars or Place d'Armes garage
    Details

    SEE THE PARKING SECTION BELOW BEFORE YOU ARRIVE

    Do not attempt to drive around Old Montréal looking for a space — the streets are one-way, narrow, and ticketed aggressively. Go straight to an underground garage (Champ-de-Mars or Place d'Armes) or leave the car where you are staying and take the Metro in. Everything in Old Montréal is walkable from there.

  14. ↓ on foot from here — about 2 km total
  15. 814:45Place d'ArmesStart of the Old Montréal walk
    Details

    ABOUT 2 KM TOTAL · COBBLESTONES, WEAR REAL SHOES

    Start at Place d'Armes, then straight into Notre-Dame Basilica — the deep-blue vaulted interior is the single most photographed room in the city. Visiting hours run roughly 09:00–16:00 Mon–Sat, adult admission around $16, so get in before four. Out the door, head down Rue Saint-Paul (oldest street in the city), through Place Jacques-Cartier where the street performers set up, past Bonsecours Market, and finish on the Old Port waterfront looking across at the Habitat 67 concrete stack.

  16. 915:00Notre-Dame Basilica≈$16 · last entry 16:00
  17. 1015:45Rue Saint-PaulOldest street in the city
  18. 1116:15Place Jacques-CartierStreet performers · terrasses
  19. 1216:45Bonsecours MarketThe silver dome
  20. 1317:15Old Port & Habitat 67 viewWaterfront quays
  21. ↓ drive 15m up the mountain
  22. 1418:45Kondiaronk Belvedere, Mount RoyalSunset ≈19:25 · the skyline photo
    Details

    FREE · PAID LOT AT THE CHALET, OR WALK UP FROM PEEL ST

    The view of the entire downtown skyline with the river behind it, from the terrace beside the Mount Royal Chalet. Sunset on 5 September is around 19:25 — be up there by 18:45 for the good light. This is the photo everyone brings home from Montréal.

  23. ↓ drive 15m back down to the Plateau
  24. 1520:00Dinner — Schwartz's or RomadosSmoked meat, or Portuguese chicken for four
    Details

    SEE THE FOOD SECTION FOR THE FULL LIST

    Two honest options for a group of four. Schwartz's on Saint-Laurent for the smoked meat sandwich that made the city famous — expect a queue down the block, it moves faster than it looks. Or Romados in the Plateau for charcoal Portuguese chicken with fries and rice, which will feed four of you enormously for very little.

  25. 1621:30Cité Mémoire, Old MontréalFree · Wed–Sun after nightfall
    Details

    FREE · WEDNESDAY TO SUNDAY, FROM NIGHTFALL

    Nine large-scale historical scenes projected onto the walls, alleys and ground of Old Montréal after dark. It went dark at the end of 2024 and returned in May 2026, running Wednesday through Sunday — Saturday night qualifies. It is free, it is genuinely striking, and almost no first-time visitor knows about it. Finish the night with a late poutine at La Banquise, open 24 hours.

  26. 1722:30La Banquise — late poutineOpen 24 hours · then sleep
Day 2 · Sunday 6 September Montréal → Québec City 345 KM · 3H 40M
  1. 1807:30St-Viateur Bagel, Mile EndOpen 24h · eat one hot, buy a dozen
    Details

    OPEN 24 HOURS · CASH-FRIENDLY · ABOUT $1 A BAGEL

    Montréal bagels are boiled in honey water and baked in a wood-fired oven — thinner, sweeter and denser than the New York kind. Get them straight out of the oven, still hot, sesame. Buy a bag for the car. Fairmount Bagel is four minutes away and the rivalry is a genuine city argument; if you have the appetite, buy one of each and settle it yourselves.

  2. 1908:15Mile End murals & Café OlimpicoOn foot · Saint-Viateur to Saint-Laurent
    Details

    SAINT-VIATEUR / SAINT-LAURENT / BERNARD

    The neighbourhood locals will tell you is the actual soul of Montréal. Café Olimpico for an espresso standing up, then walk Saint-Laurent to see the murals left behind by the annual Mural Festival — some of them cover entire five-storey walls. Vintage shops, record stores, and the outdoor staircases the city is known for.

  3. ↓ drive 10m
  4. 2009:15Marché Jean-Talon, Little ItalyCheese curds · maple · cider for the car
    Details

    ONE OF THE LARGEST OPEN-AIR MARKETS IN NORTH AMERICA

    Early September is peak season — the stalls are stacked with Québec produce, and this is the right place to buy fresh cheese curds (they should squeak against your teeth), maple butter, and cider for the car. Le Marché des Saveurs at the north end sells only Québec-made products and is the best souvenir shopping in the city.

  5. 2110:15Leave Montréal — Autoroute 40 EastEarlier now, to fit the canyon in · A-40, not Route 138
    Details

    A-40 IS FASTER · ROUTE 138 IS PRETTIER AND TWICE AS LONG

    Take the A-40. The scenic alternative — Chemin du Roy / Route 138, the oldest road in Canada, running through riverside villages — is beautiful but realistically doubles the drive. Note it for a future trip.

  6. ↓ 145 km · 1h 30m
  7. 2212:30Trois-RivièresOptional — you cannot do this AND the canyon; pick one
    Details

    EXACTLY HALFWAY · RUE DES URSULINES

    The second-oldest city in Québec, and a pleasant 45-minute leg stretch. Rue des Ursulines is a preserved colonial street, and the riverside promenade looks out over the widest part of the St. Lawrence. Skip it if you would rather have more time at the falls.

  8. ↓ 130 km · 1h 20m
  9. ↓ 300 km · 3h · A-40 then Rte 138, straight past Québec City
  10. 2313:15Canyon Sainte-Anne74 m gorge · 3 suspension bridges · last entry 16:00
    Details

    BEAUPRÉ · 30 MIN PAST MONTMORENCY ON RTE 138

    A 74-metre waterfall dropping into a granite gorge, crossed by three suspension bridges — the highest hangs about 60 m above the water. Open April to October, so early September is fine.

    Take this one before Montmorency, not after. It is the furthest point of the day, so you do it first and pick up Montmorency on the way back into the city. Last entry here is 16:00 and Montmorency shuts at 16:30 — get the order wrong and you lose one of them.

    Adult admission is roughly $15–30 depending on the source, so check the current rate before you go. Allow about an hour and a half.

  11. 2415:15Montmorency Falls≈$13.90 · closes 16:30 — go straight here from the canyon
    Details

    PARC DE LA CHUTE-MONTMORENCY · 15 MIN PAST QUÉBEC CITY ON RTE 138

    83 metres tall — higher than Niagara — with a suspension bridge straight across the crest and a panoramic staircase down the cliff face. Adult admission is about $13.90 in high season, the cable car about $15 return, parking included with entry.

    Critical timing: from 19 August the park closes at 16:30. Arriving at 14:30 gives you a comfortable two hours. Arriving at 16:00 gets you nothing. Do it today, not Monday — Monday morning belongs to the drive.

  12. ↓ 45 km · 40m back into the old city
  13. 2516:45Québec City — park in Lower TownVieux-Port / Bassin Louise · don't drive inside the walls
  14. ↓ on foot — lower town first, then climb. Everything below is walking order.
  15. 2617:00Place Royale & Notre-Dame-des-VictoiresGoblinChamplain's 1608 site · Eun-tak window-shopping scene
    Details

    PARK IN LOWER TOWN · WALK UPHILL FROM HERE · NO BACKTRACKING

    Start where you parked. Place Royale is where Champlain founded the city in 1608; round the corner is the Fresque des Québécois, a five-storey trompe-l'œil mural that looks like a real street until you touch it. Then Rue du Petit-Champlain, the narrow flower-strung lane that fills every Québec feed you have ever scrolled — and, at roughly number 68, the red door from Goblin. It is a working private doorway, so photograph it without blocking it.

  16. 2717:15Fresque des QuébécoisGoblinFive-storey mural · glimpsed in the chase scene
  17. 2817:25Rue du Petit-ChamplainGoblinOldest commercial street in North America
  18. 2917:40The Red DoorGoblin ★≈68 Rue du Petit Champlain · the portal to Canada
  19. 3017:55Escalier Casse-CouGoblinBreakneck Steps · climb up · funicular ≈$5 if knees object
    Details

    FUNICULAR ≈$5 IF ANYONE'S KNEES OBJECT

    The Escalier Casse-Cou — "Breakneck Steps" — is the direct climb. At the top you cross Porte Prescott, then it is two minutes to Parc Montmorency on the ramparts (a park in the old city, not the waterfall). Carry on to Rue de Buade for La Boutique de Noël, which sells Christmas year-round, and Rue du Trésor, where artists sell prints in an alley barely two metres wide.

  20. 3118:10Porte PrescottGoblinCôte de la Montagne · the pedestrian bridge scene
  21. 3218:20Parc MontmorencyGoblinRampart-wall scene · NOT the waterfall — a park in the old city
  22. 3318:35La Boutique de NoëlGoblin47 Rue de Buade · Christmas year-round · check closing time
  23. 3418:50Rue du TrésorArtists' alley, two metres wide
  24. 3519:05Château FrontenacGoblinThe "Goblin hotel" · go into the lobby
    Details

    ONE CONTINUOUS LINE ALONG THE CLIFF TOP

    Walk into the Château Frontenac lobby — you do not need to be a guest — then out onto the Terrasse Dufferin boardwalk above the river, with the Jardin des Gouverneurs tucked behind the hotel. The boardwalk continues as Terrasse Pierre-Dugua-de-Mons and climbs to Parc du Bastion-de-la-Reine by the Citadelle, which has the best view in the city. Finish by dropping out of the Saint-Louis Gate to the Fontaine de Tourny, floodlit at dusk.

  25. 3619:25Terrasse Dufferin & Jardin des GouverneursGoblinBoardwalk above the river · garden tucked behind the Château
  26. 3719:45Pierre-Dugua-de-Mons → Parc du Bastion-de-la-ReineGoblinUphill toward the Citadelle · best view in the city
  27. 3820:10Fontaine de TournyGoblin ★Outside Saint-Louis Gate · lit at dusk · the confession scene
  28. 3920:30Dinner — Chez Ashton or Aux Anciens CanadiensClassic poutine, or tourtière in a 1675 house
    Details

    SEE THE FOOD SECTION

    Chez Ashton is the local institution and does the classic version with no cleverness attached. Aux Anciens Canadiens, in a house built in 1675, is where to eat tourtière and maple-glazed duck if you want the proper Québécois menu. Le Buffet de l'Antiquaire is the cheap, honest, locals' diner option.

  29. 4021:45Old Québec after darkRue Saint-Louis · Rue Saint-Jean · the lit ramparts
    Details

    FREE · JUST WALK

    The day-trippers have gone, the stone streets are lit, and the Château is floodlit above the river. Walk Rue Saint-Louis and Rue Saint-Jean, then back along the Terrasse Dufferin. If anyone still has legs, the Promenade des Gouverneurs — 310 steps climbing the cliff behind the Château to the Plains of Abraham — is spectacular and almost empty at night.

Day 3 · Monday 7 September · Labour Day Québec City → Scarborough 805 KM · 8H 15M
  1. 4106:15Breakfast — Le Buffet de l'AntiquaireOpens ≈06:00 · or eat Paillard pastries in the car
    Details

    LE BUFFET DE L'ANTIQUAIRE OPENS ≈ 06:00

    The Lower Town diner opens early and does breakfast poutine and eggs for very little. Alternatively, buy pastries from Paillard on Rue Saint-Jean the night before and eat them in the car. Do not go looking for breakfast at 07:30 — that is how the departure slips.

  2. 4207:00Depart Québec City — Autoroute 20 WestHard deadline · this is the one fixed time of the trip
    Details

    TAKE THE A-30 SOUTH SHORE BYPASS AROUND MONTRÉAL

    Do not drive through the island of Montréal. The A-30 runs south of the city and rejoins the A-20 west of it — it avoids the bridges, the tunnel and the permanent construction. There is a short tolled section on the A-30 near Beauharnois (a couple of dollars, billed by plate); it is worth it, but you can also stay on the A-20 through the city if you would rather pay nothing.

  3. ↓ 255 km · 2h 45m
  4. 4310:00Drummondville area — fuel & first breakHalf-tank here, fill properly in Ontario
    Details

    ANYWHERE AROUND DRUMMONDVILLE OR THE A-30

    Twenty minutes, legs stretched, tank filled. Gas in Québec is usually a little dearer than Ontario, so a half-tank here and a full one in Cornwall is the cheap play.

  5. ↓ 100 km · 1h · A-30 South Shore bypass
  6. 4411:00A-30 around MontréalSkips the bridges, tunnel and island traffic
  7. ↓ 160 km · 1h 40m · cross into Ontario
  8. 4512:15Morrisburg — Upper Canada VillageLunch · Long Sault Parkway picnic · Exit 758
    Details

    401 EXIT 758 · THE STOP YOU SKIPPED ON SATURDAY

    Here is where Saturday's optional stop pays off. A recreated 1860s Canadian village with working mills, farms and costumed interpreters, right off the highway. Even if you skip the paid site, the Long Sault Parkway nearby island-hops across the St. Lawrence and makes a beautiful free picnic stop with the bagels you still have in the trunk.

  9. ↓ 145 km · 1h 30m
  10. 4614:30Kingston or Gananoque — last breakSwap drivers · check Ontario 511 before the final leg
    Details

    LAST GOOD COFFEE BEFORE THE HOME STRETCH

    Swap drivers here if you are sharing. From Kingston it is a straight 260 km run home. This is the point where you make the call on the final stretch — see the note below.

  11. ↓ 260 km · 2h 45m, longer if the 401 is stacked
  12. 4717:30Home — Scarborough17:30–19:00 depending on Labour Day traffic
    Details

    DEPENDS ENTIRELY ON THE 401 WESTBOUND

    Labour Day Monday afternoon is when every cottage in eastern Ontario drives back to Toronto at once. Check Ontario 511 before you leave Kingston. If the 401 is stacked from Oshawa in, dropping onto Highway 2 through Port Hope and Cobourg for a stretch is slower on paper and often faster in practice.

City one

Montréal — what to actually see

You have one afternoon and one morning. The list below is split into what everyone sees and what people who live there send visitors to instead. On a first trip, do most of the first list and pick two from the second.

The famous ones

Old Montréal

Notre-Dame Basilica★ Must

A cobalt-blue vaulted ceiling lit with thousands of gold stars — nothing about photographs prepares you for it.

More

The evening AURA light-and-orchestra show inside the basilica is a separate ticket and worth it if the timing works.

≈$16 adult · Mon–Sat 09:00–16:00, Sun 12:30–16:00 · 45 min Map
Old Montréal

Rue Saint-Paul & Place Jacques-Cartier★ Must

The oldest street in the city, cobbled end to end, running into the square where the street performers, terrasses and flower stalls are. Bonsecours Market's silver dome anchors the east end.

Free · best late afternoon · 1–2 hrs Map
Mont-Royal

Kondiaronk Belvedere★ Must

Designed by the same landscape architect as Central Park. The terrace by the Chalet gives you the whole downtown skyline with the river behind it. Sunset is the moment.

Free · paid parking at the Chalet · 1 hr Map
Côte-des-Neiges

Saint Joseph's Oratory

The largest church in Canada, with a dome visible from most of the city and 283 wooden steps that pilgrims still climb on their knees. The view from the terrace rivals Mount Royal and far fewer visitors bother.

Free entry · donation suggested · 1 hr Map
Little Italy

Marché Jean-Talon★ Must

One of the biggest open-air markets in North America and at its absolute best in early September. Cheese curds, maple everything, Québec cider, and enough free samples to constitute a second breakfast.

Free · open daily · 45 min Map
Old Port

The waterfront & Habitat 67

Walk the quays for the view across to Habitat 67, the stacked-concrete apartment experiment from Expo 67 that still looks like it arrived from the future. Ferris wheel, zip line and boat tours if you want them.

Free to walk · 45 min Map
Hochelaga

Olympic Park & Botanical Garden

The leaning Olympic tower is the tallest of its kind in the world, with an observatory at the top.

More

Next door, the Botanical Garden and the Biodôme are a half-day if you want one — realistically a "next trip" for this weekend.

Paid · needs 3+ hrs · skip if short Map
Downtown

The Underground City (RÉSO)

33 km of connected tunnels, malls and Metro stations under downtown. A curiosity in September, a lifesaver in January — but worth ducking into once just to see the scale of it.

Free · 30 min · rainy-day backup Map

Hidden gems

After dark · free

Cité Mémoire

Historical scenes projected onto the walls and alleys of Old Montréal once night falls. Returned in May 2026 with nine scenes after being dark for a year.

More

Runs Wednesday to Sunday. Almost no visitor knows it exists.

Free · Wed–Sun from nightfall · 1 hr Map
Mile End

The murals & the Van Horne overpass

The annual Mural Festival leaves entire building walls painted. The pedestrian overpass at Van Horne is where locals go for the sunset view back over the neighbourhood — an ordinary bridge with an extraordinary outlook.

Free · golden hour · 1 hr walk Map
Plateau Mont-Royal

The exterior spiral staircases

The wrought-iron staircases curling up the front of every triplex are the single most Montréal thing there is — a 19th-century tax-and-bylaw quirk that became the city's signature.

More

Rue Saint-Denis, Duluth and Marquette are the best blocks.

Free · just walk · 30 min Map
Plateau

Ruelles vertes — the green alleys

Hundreds of back lanes have been torn up by residents and replanted into shared gardens with murals, benches and vines.

More

You will not find them on a tourist map; duck into any alley off Rue Rachel or Marquette and see what you get.

Free · residential — be quiet · 20 min Map
Sud-Ouest

Lachine Canal & Atwater Market

A 14 km waterside path along the old industrial canal, ending at Atwater Market's clock tower.

More

Rent BIXI bikes and do the flattest, prettiest ride in the city. Locals rate it over the Old Port and they are right.

Free path · BIXI ≈$1 + per min · 1.5 hrs Map
Plateau

Parc La Fontaine

Where the Plateau actually spends its Sunday. Ponds, a bandstand, enormous trees, people playing pétanque badly.

More

Bring bagels and the market cheese and eat on the grass — the most Montréal hour you can have for nothing.

Free · 1 hr · picnic here Map
Parc Jean-Drapeau

The Biosphère

Buckminster Fuller's giant geodesic sphere on the island in the river, left over from Expo 67.

More

Reachable by Metro in ten minutes and it looks like nothing else on earth. The island also gives you the best skyline view from water level.

Free to view · Metro Jean-Drapeau · 1 hr Map
Downtown

Chinatown & the Quartier des Spectacles

The paifang gates on Saint-Laurent lead into a compact, busy Chinatown that does hand-pulled noodles better than the price suggests.

More

A block north, the Quartier des Spectacles usually has something free and outdoors running on a long weekend.

Free · check listings for the weekend · 1 hr Map
City two

Québec City — what to actually see

Old Québec is small. You can cross the entire walled city on foot in twenty minutes, which means an afternoon and an evening is genuinely enough to see it properly rather than rush it.

The famous ones

Upper Town

Château Frontenac & Terrasse Dufferin★ Must

The most photographed hotel on earth, and the boardwalk terrace beneath it running along the cliff edge above the river. You do not need to be a guest — walk in through the lobby, then walk the terrace at dusk.

Free · guided tours available · 1 hr Map
Lower Town

Quartier Petit-Champlain★ Must

The oldest commercial street in North America — a narrow lane of stone buildings, boutiques and hanging flowers under the cliff.

More

It is as crowded as it is beautiful; go early evening once the day-trip buses have gone.

Free · funicular ≈$5 · 1 hr Map
Lower Town

Place Royale & the Fresque des Québécois★ Must

The exact spot Champlain founded the city in 1608, with the little stone church of Notre-Dame-des-Victoires on the square.

More

Round the corner, a five-storey painted mural of 400 years of Québec history that fools you until you get close.

Free · 45 min Map
Beaupré · stop 23

Canyon Sainte-Anne

A 74-metre waterfall falling into a granite gorge, crossed by three suspension bridges — the highest around 60 m above the water.

More

Thirty minutes past Montmorency on Route 138, which makes it the furthest point of your Sunday. Take it first and collect Montmorency on the way back. Open April to October. Last entry is 16:00 and Montmorency closes at 16:30, so the order matters. Allow about 90 minutes.

≈$15–30 · last entry 16:00 · 1.5 hrs Map
Beauport

Montmorency Falls★ Must

83 m, higher than Niagara, with a suspension bridge over the top and a staircase down the cliff. Fifteen minutes from the old city and the best half-day outside the walls.

≈$13.90 adult · cable car ≈$15 · closes 16:30 from 19 Aug Map
Upper Town

La Citadelle & the walls

A star-shaped fortress still garrisoned by the Royal 22e Régiment, sitting on the highest point of the city.

More

In summer there is a changing of the guard, complete with the regimental goat. You can also just walk the ramparts for free.

Ramparts free · fort tour paid · 1–2 hrs Map
Upper Town

Plains of Abraham

The battlefield that decided the fate of New France in 1759, now an enormous clifftop park. Great for a walk, a picnic, or simply the view down the St.

More

Lawrence. Free and rarely crowded away from the main paths.

Free · 1 hr · flat and easy Map
Parliament Hill

Fontaine de Tourny & the Parliament Building

A 19th-century Bordeaux fountain gifted to the city, in front of the Second Empire parliament. Lit beautifully at night and only two minutes outside the Saint-Louis Gate — an easy add-on to the evening walk.

Free · best after dark · 20 min Map
Upper Town

Rue du Trésor & Rue Saint-Jean

Rue du Trésor is a two-metre-wide alley where artists have sold prints since the 1950s. Rue Saint-Jean is the main commercial street — bakeries, chocolate, bars, and much better value than the streets right by the Château.

Free · 45 min Map

Hidden gems

Best value in the city

The Lévis ferry★ Must

A 12-minute crossing to the far bank for about $4.50. From the middle of the river you get the view of the Château Frontenac on its cliff that every helicopter photo is trying to copy — for the price of a coffee.

More

Stay on and come straight back. Runs from 06:00 until after 02:00.

≈$4.50 return-ish · 30 min total · do this Map
Saint-Roch

Quartier Saint-Roch

Ten minutes downhill from the walls and where people who live in Québec City actually eat and drink.

More

Rue Saint-Joseph has the microbreweries, the good bakeries and the record shops — and prices roughly a third below the tourist streets.

Free to wander · dinner here to save money Map
Behind the Château

Promenade des Gouverneurs

310 steps up a boardwalk staircase clinging to the cliff between the Terrasse Dufferin and the Plains of Abraham. Steep, empty and the best river view in the city. Skip it if anyone in the group has bad knees.

Free · 310 steps · 30 min Map
Upper Town

Morrin Centre

Guardian: The Lonely and Great God

The Goblin trail

Québec City is the drama's Canadian location, and almost all of it sits inside the walled city — which means you can walk the whole trail in one evening without changing the itinerary. Sunday's route (stops 26–38) already runs through it in geographic order.

One expectation to reset

Goblin was shot in autumn — red maples, fallen leaves, the leaf-catching scene. You are arriving on 5–7 September, when Québec's trees are still green. Colour here peaks early-to-mid October. The buildings, streets and doors will look exactly like the drama; the foliage will not.

The two most people come for

The portal

The Red Door★ Must

The door Kim Shin and Ji Eun-tak step through to arrive in Canada, and the single most-photographed spot on the trail.

More

Sources list it as 68 and 71 Rue du Petit Champlain — the two are metres apart, so you will find it either way. It is a working private doorway: photograph it, don't block it. A recreated red door has been put up nearby specifically for photos.

≈68 Rue du Petit Champlain · stop 29 · expect a queue Map
The confession

Fontaine de Tourny★ Must

The fountain in front of the Parliament Building where Kim Shin admits to himself that Eun-tak is his first love — the scene most fans name as their favourite.

More

Just outside the Saint-Louis Gate, five minutes from the Château, and floodlit after dark. Your Sunday slot at 19:40 puts you there right at dusk.

Place de l'Assemblée-Nationale · stop 38 · free · best at dusk Map

The terrace where the pair share a casual meal. It continues on from Dufferin Terrace toward the Citadelle, so it is simply the path you take to reach the Bastion — no detour at all.

My honest advice: skip it. The scene is about autumn leaves, and in early September there will not be any. It also spends 15 minutes of the one morning where the schedule has no slack.

How to actually walk it

  • One continuous uphill line, no backtracking: Lower Town → Breakneck Steps → Upper Town → Château → terraces → fountain. That is exactly stops 26–38.
  • Budget 3½ hours with photo stops.
  • Short on time? Protect the Red Door and the Fontaine de Tourny.

Three things that will improve every photo you take this weekend

  • Skip midday. Both old towns are stone canyons — at noon, half blinding highlight, half black shadow. Sunset ≈19:25 Sat, ≈19:15 Sun.
  • Go before 09:00 for Petit-Champlain, Dufferin and Place Jacques-Cartier. Packed the rest of the weekend.
  • Turn around. The crowd faces one way. Shoot the Old Port inland, Petit-Champlain back up the stairs, Dufferin at the Château.
The whole point of the trip

What you have to eat

Both cities have two or three dishes they genuinely invented, and a lot of places selling mediocre versions of them to visitors. Below is the split between the famous name, the version locals actually rate, and roughly what it costs.

Montréal

The one you cannot skip

Smoked meat on rye★ Must

Beef brisket cured for ten days, smoked, steamed, hand-cut and piled on rye with yellow mustard.

More

Schwartz's (3895 St-Laurent) has done it since 1928 and the queue is part of it. Ask for medium fat — that is the correct answer. To skip the line: Main Deli is directly across the street, and Snowdon Deli is where locals go.

≈$14–20 · cash preferred at Schwartz's · queue 20–40 min Map
Breakfast, non-negotiable

Montréal bagels★ Must

Boiled in honey water, baked in a wood oven, thinner and sweeter than New York's. St-Viateur and Fairmount are both open 24 hours and four minutes apart in Mile End.

More

Eat one hot from the oven with nothing on it, then buy a dozen for the car.

≈$1.20 each · open 24h · sesame is the default Map
The national dish

Poutine at La Banquise★ Must

Fries, squeaky cheese curds, hot gravy. La Banquise (994 Rachel Est) has served it 24 hours a day for decades with 30-odd variations — La Taquise with guacamole is the cult one, the plain classique is the honest one.

More

Perfect at midnight after Mount Royal.

≈$12–18 · open 24h · vegan option exists Map
Best value for four

Romados — Portuguese chicken

A Plateau counter with charcoal grills going all day. Half a chicken, piri-piri, fries and rice for a fraction of restaurant prices, and portions that defeat most people.

More

This is the smartest dinner in the city for a group on a budget.

≈$12–16 a head · takeout · queue at dinner Map

≈$6–8 · lunch only · no substitutions, ever Map

Drink local

One note on maple taffy

Tire d'érable — hot maple syrup poured on snow and rolled onto a stick — is the great Québec sweet, but it is a March and April thing at the sugar shacks. In September you will find it at a few tourist stands and on Île d'Orléans, but do not build a day around chasing it.

The part that ruins trips

Parking, driving & not getting ticketed

You are arriving in two cities with narrow historic cores, aggressive parking enforcement and signage in French. Twenty minutes of reading now saves a $120 ticket and an hour of circling.

The rule that catches every Ontario driver

Right turn on a red light is illegal everywhere on the island of Montréal. It is legal in the rest of Québec, and legal in Ontario, which is exactly why visitors do it out of habit and get ticketed. On the island: red means stop, full stop.

Montréal

Best option

Underground garages near Old Montréal

Head for the garages around Champ-de-Mars, Place d'Armes and Complexe Desjardins rather than the waterfront lots, which charge a premium for the view.

More

Book a spot in advance through a parking app on a long weekend — Old Montréal fills up.

≈$15–30/day · secure · walk to everything Map
Cheapest by far

Park at a Metro station and ride in

Leave the car at a park-and-ride — Namur, Angrignon or Longueuil on the south shore — and take the Metro downtown in 15–30 minutes.

More

With four of you the fares still beat downtown parking, and the car sits somewhere far safer than a street space.

Lot free or a few $ · Metro fare per person · saves the most Map
Street parking

Read the sign. Then read it again.

Montréal's signs stack multiple rules on one post, in French, and permit-only zones (marked with a letter and number) will get you towed, not just ticketed.

More

Meters are paid by licence plate through the city's parking app — payment follows the plate, so you can move between paid streets on the same session.

≈$3–4.50/hr · towing is real · avoid if unsure
Security

Empty the car, every time

Both cities are safe to walk at night by North American standards, and both have opportunistic vehicle break-ins.

More

A car with Ontario plates and visible luggage is the obvious target. Nothing on the seats, nothing in the footwells, bags in the boot before you park — not after.

Underground > street · always

Québec City

Free after 21:00

On-street parking is only paid 09:00–21:00

This is the single best thing to know about Québec City. Street meters run daily 09:00 to 21:00; outside those hours, including all night, street parking is free.

More

Pay by plate through the city app and you can move between paid streets on one session.

Free 21:00–09:00 · pay by plate · check signs for cleaning days

Park in Lower Town, walk up

The lots around the Vieux-Port / Marché du Vieux-Port and Bassin Louise are consistently cheaper and easier than anything inside the walls, and they put you two minutes from Place Royale and Petit-Champlain.

Cheaper than Upper Town · flat walk to Lower Town Map

Don't drive inside the walls

Old Québec's streets are narrow, one-way, cobbled, closed in places to traffic, and full of pedestrians who assume no car is coming.

More

Park once, outside or below, and walk. The entire walled city is about a twenty-minute walk end to end.

Included · arrive by 14:30 · closes 16:30 Map

Cheapest to most expensive — pick from the top

FREE Québec City · Parc-O-Bus park-and-rideThe cheapest option in either city, and almost nobody visiting knows about it. Québec City runs free park-and-ride lots outside downtown, all served by bus routes into Old Québec and Sainte-Foy. Park free, ride in, and never think about the car again.
FREE Québec City · any street meter after 21:00On-street parking is charged 09:00–21:00 daily only. Outside those hours — including all night — street parking is free. If you arrive after nine, do not pay anything. Check the sign for street-cleaning days.
FREE Montréal · residential streets with no red squareMost Montréal side streets are free with no time limit outside posted hours. The trick is reading the sign correctly — see the decoder below. Ten minutes' walk from Old Montréal is a different world price-wise.
≈$0–5 Montréal · Metro park-and-ride + fareLeave the car at Namur, Angrignon or Longueuil and ride in for 15–30 minutes. With four of you the fares still beat a downtown garage, and the car sits somewhere far safer than a street space.
≈$3–4.50
/hr Metered street parking, either cityPay by licence plate through the city app in both cities — payment follows the plate, so you can move between paid streets on the same session without paying twice.
≈$12–20
/day Québec City · Lower Town lotsVieux-Port / Marché du Vieux-Port / Bassin Louise. Consistently cheaper and easier than anything inside the walls, and two minutes from Place Royale — which is exactly where your Sunday walk starts.
≈$15–30
/day Montréal · Old Montréal underground garagesChamp-de-Mars, Place d'Armes, Complexe Desjardins. Secure and central, and the most you should ever pay. Book ahead on a long weekend. The waterfront lots charge a premium for the location — walk two blocks inland instead.
$250+ Misreading a Montréal signTickets run $42 for an expired meter to $148 for a bus or hydrant zone. Add a $130 tow plus $26 a day storage and one bad guess costs more than the whole weekend's parking. When the sign is ambiguous, drive on.

Decoding a Montréal parking sign

Montréal stacks several rules on one pole, in French, and gets more parking revenue out of visitors than it probably should. Four things tell you everything:

P

Green P with an arrowParking is allowed, during the hours listed, in the direction the arrow points. Outside those hours the default applies — which on most Montréal streets means free, no time limit.

✕

Red circle with a slashNo parking during the hours shown. If it also carries a tow symbol, they mean it — this is the one that costs $130 plus storage.

55

A small red square with a numberPermit-holders only. This is the single most common visitor mistake. If you see a red square with a zone number in the corner, that stretch is not for you — park where the sign has no red square.

↑

The arrow directionThe rule applies only to the side of the pole the arrow points to. Two signs pointing opposite ways on one pole means two different rules for the two halves of the block. Read the whole stack top to bottom — the top sign wins during its hours.

The other rules that catch Ontario drivers

  • No right turn on red on the island of Montréal. Legal everywhere else you drive — which is why visitors do it on autopilot.
  • Street cleaning tows, it doesn't ticket. Temporary orange signs override every permanent one. If one appeared, move the car.
  • Signs are French only. Sauf=except · lun–dim=Mon–Sun · livraison=deliveries · remorquage=towing.

Where to base yourselves (cheap and easy to park)

Montréal: the Quartier Latin and the eastern edge of the Plateau are central, walkable and cheaper than Old Montréal. For the lowest total cost with a car, look at Longueuil or the south shore — parking is free or nearly, and the Metro puts you downtown in fifteen minutes.

Québec City: inside the walls is the most expensive ground in the province on a long weekend. Sainte-Foy (about 15 minutes out, near the train station) and Lévis (across the river, and you get the ferry ride as a bonus) are meaningfully cheaper and usually come with free parking. Saint-Roch is the compromise: walkable to the old city, distinctly cheaper, and better restaurants.

You said you are booking accommodation yourselves — the only thing worth adding is that for Labour Day weekend, filter by "free parking" before you filter by price. A cheaper room that costs $30 a night to park beside is not cheaper.

Where to stop for petrol and a meal

Fuel & food on the road

Ontario has proper service centres right on the highway. Québec does not. That single difference is the thing to plan around, and the map below is laid out so you can see it at a glance.

Save both to your phone — they work with no signal

The mistake that catches people

  • ONroutes serve one direction only. Newcastle, Trenton North, Napanee, Mallorytown North, Ingleside and Bainsville are westbound — you cannot use them on Saturday, only coming home Monday.
  • Going out you have Port Hope, Trenton South, Odessa, Mallorytown South and Morrisburg. That is plenty.
  • Québec has no equivalent. Its haltes routières are washrooms and picnic tables, no fuel and no food. You buy petrol at town exits.

Looking for McDonald's?

  • There isn't one at any ONroute. Their brands are Tim Hortons, Starbucks, Burger King, Subway, Popeyes, A&W, New York Fries and Booster Juice.
  • For McDonald's you come off at a town — Cobourg, Belleville, Kingston, Brockville, Cornwall in Ontario, then Berthierville and Trois-Rivières in Québec.
  • It costs about five minutes each way off the highway.

Rough fuel estimate

About 1,690 km. A mid-size car at roughly 8.5 L/100 km burns about 145 litres — call it $220–260 in fuel for the weekend, split four ways. Fill in Ontario where you can; Québec pump prices usually run a little higher.

Tolls: none required. The 401, A-20 and A-40 are all free. The only toll you might touch is the short A-30 bypass south of Montréal on Monday — a couple of dollars, billed by plate, and worth it to skip the island.

Language

Québec is French-first

Everyone in tourist areas speaks English and will switch the moment they hear you. Opening with bonjour rather than hi is a small courtesy that visibly changes how you are treated, especially outside the old towns.

More

Road signs are French only — arrêt is stop, sortie is exit, ouest is west.

Try the greeting · it genuinely matters
Weather

Warm days, cold evenings

Early September in Québec City means pleasant afternoons and evenings that drop to around 10–12 °C, with wind off the river on the Terrasse Dufferin.

More

Bring a real jacket, not just a hoodie. Cobblestones everywhere: proper shoes, no new sandals.

Layers + walking shoes
Time & money

No time change, same currency

Québec is on Eastern Time exactly like Ontario — no clock change at the border. Cards are accepted almost everywhere, but carry some cash: Schwartz's and a few older counters prefer it.

More

Tipping is 15–20%, same as home.

ET both sides · carry ≈$50 cash
Before you leave

Check both 511 services

Ontario 511 for the 401, and Québec 511 for the A-20/A-40 — Québec runs enormous summer construction programmes and a single closure can add an hour.

More

Check Monday morning before you pull out of Québec City, and again at Kingston.

Check twice on Monday
Labour Day Monday

What is open

Major attractions, restaurants and the old towns run normal or holiday hours. Some smaller independent shops close.

More

It does not affect this itinerary much — you are on the road by seven — but do not count on a leisurely 09:00 café stop.

Eat early or buy the night before
Book now

Three things worth reserving

Accommodation in both cities (it will sell out). Dinner at Aux Anciens Canadiens if you want the traditional meal.

More

And Onhwa' Lumina at Wendake if you decide to add it. Everything else on this page can be done by turning up.

Beds first, today
The one social rule

"Bonjour, hi" — and what you say back

You will be greeted with "Bonjour, hi" constantly in Montréal. It is an offer of both languages, and whichever one you answer in is the one they will use for the rest of the conversation.

More

Nobody minds you choosing English. Saying bonjour first and then switching is the move that reliably gets you treated well.

Answer in either · the greeting itself is the courtesy
Don't do this

Two things that land badly

Comparing everything to how it is done at home, and assuming everyone will switch to English without being asked.

More

Neither city is remotely hostile — but both notice. The other common miss is never leaving the old town: the best food in both cities is a fifteen-minute walk outside the tourist core.

Ask before assuming · then walk further than the map suggests
Buying alcohol

Beer in shops, spirits in the SAQ

Beer and cider are sold in ordinary corner shops (dépanneurs) and supermarkets until 23:00 — a genuine novelty coming from Ontario.

More

Wine and spirits come from the government SAQ stores only. Legal drinking age in Québec is 18, not 19.

Dépanneur for beer · SAQ for the rest
Paying

Tax, tipping and cash

Listed prices exclude tax — expect about 15% added at the till. Tipping is 15–20% as at home, and card terminals will prompt you.

More

Carry ≈$50 cash between you: Schwartz's and a few older counters still prefer it.

+15% tax · 15–20% tip · some cash
Getting around

Leave the car, take the Metro

Montréal's Metro reaches almost everywhere you want on this trip, and where it doesn't a bus will.

More

Buy a day pass rather than singles if you are making more than three trips. Québec City needs no transit at all — the walled city is twenty minutes end to end on foot.

Day pass beats singles after ~3 rides

Six phrases that cover almost everything

BonjourHello — open every single interaction with this. bon-ZHOOR
Parlez-vous anglais ?Do you speak English? The polite way to switch. par-lay VOO on-GLAY
Merci beaucoupThank you very much. mair-SEE bo-KOO
L'addition, s'il vous plaîtThe bill, please. la-dee-see-OHN seel-voo-PLAY
Où est le stationnement ?Where is the parking? oo ay luh sta-syon-MON
Une poutine, s'il vous plaîtThe most important sentence in this document. oon poo-TEEN

How this was put together. Routes and drive times from mapping data along Highway 401 / Autoroute 20 and 40. Attractions, food, photo spots and parking rules cross-checked across the Québec City and Montréal tourism boards, the Ville de Montréal and Ville de Québec parking pages, local city guides, travel forums and community recommendation threads, plus write-ups aggregating what circulates on Reddit, TikTok and Instagram. I could not read TikTok, Instagram or X directly — no access to them — so anything sourced from those platforms reached this page second-hand through published round-ups, and is flagged as popular rather than verified. Prices and hours were current as of late August 2026.

Verify before you rely on it. Opening hours, admission prices and ferry schedules change, and Labour Day weekend hours can differ from the published ones. Confirm anything time-critical — Montmorency Falls closing at 16:30, Notre-Dame Basilica's last entry, and Cité Mémoire's Wednesday-to-Sunday schedule — on the operator's own site the week you travel.
